title: Deterministic min-throughput allocator with staged overload shedder
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem: Dedicated fleets currently expose coarse admission policies (token-bucket and simple queue depth caps) that cause unpredictable drops for mid-tier customers under multi-tenant burst conditions. We need a deterministic way to guarantee a configurable minimum throughput for reserved customers while still allowing headroom for best-effort traffic and enabling graceful, observable degradation when capacity is saturated.

Proposal summary: Implement a deterministic Min-Throughput Allocator (MTA) in the routing layer that reserves a floor of throughput per-customer (or per-SLA group) and enforces that reservation across autoscale and overload events. When aggregate demand exceeds physical capacity, an ordered staged shedder will run: stage 0 (soft deprioritization and latency-aware queued pacing), stage 1 (best-effort throttle of non-reserved traffic), stage 2 (targeted preemption of degraded weight classes with transparent rate-limit responses), and stage 3 (circuit ejection for healthy fallback). The allocator integrates with the autoscaler to signal desired burst headroom and with the console for SLO dashboards and cost accounting.

Key design points: deterministic reservation by sliding-window token accounting rather than opportunistic first-come-first-serve; per-fleet admission policy expressed as min_throughput (tokens/sec) + burst_headroom; admission checks run at request ingress before batching; queued pacing uses per-SLA priority queues with fairness windows to avoid starvation; shedder stages are configurable and emitted as telemetry events for post-incident analysis.

Trade-offs and decisions so far: we chose sliding-window accounting (slightly more CPU) to get deterministic guarantees and easier verification in audits; we will not rely on cross-node global locks — reservation is per-router with periodic reconciliation to a global view to avoid blowups during network partition. We debated using a centralized admission coordinator but prioritized availability and low-latency checks.

Rollout plan: alpha on a single regional Dedicated pool (us-west-2) for internal traffic, canary to two customer fleets with opt-in config, then gradual rollout to all Dedicated fleets. The allocator will default off for legacy configs.

Observability: new metrics (mta.reserved_tokens, mta.consumed_tokens, mta.stage, mta.reconciliation_errors), per-request trace tags (mta_reservation_id, mta_stage), and a console SLO view showing guaranteed vs delivered throughput over time.

Risks: incorrect reservation sizing could starve best-effort customers — mitigated via conservative defaults and canary. Reconciliation lag could temporarily oversubscribe capacity — mitigated with conservative headroom and faster reconciliation cadence.

Outcome expected: deterministic delivery of minimum committed throughput for reserved customers, predictable behavior under overload, and improved customer trust for Dedicated SLAs.

acceptance_criteria: Unit + integration tests for sliding-window allocator with deterministic assertions included
Canary deployed to a single internal Dedicated fleet and observed delivering >= 95% of configured min_throughput over 48h under synthetic overload tests
Staged shedder transitions observed in metrics and traces with human-readable reasons
Autoscaler integration: when reserved headroom calls exceed thresholds, autoscaler triggers scaled nodes and respects reservation signals
Console shows reserved vs delivered throughput and emits alerts on reconciliation_errors
